short_definition: Burnout is a state of chronic exhaustion, growing cynicism or detachment, and reduced effectiveness caused by prolonged, unmanaged stress, most commonly associated with work.
explanation: The World Health Organization's ICD-11 classification describes burnout as an occupational phenomenon, not a medical condition, caused by chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed. It is defined by three dimensions: exhaustion, increased mental distance or cynicism toward one's job, and reduced professional effectiveness. It usually builds up over months, unlike a single bad week.

Burnout matters because it can affect your health, relationships, work quality and money decisions. Examples include quitting suddenly without a plan or spending to cope with stress. Early signs often include dreading work, poor sleep, irritability, and feeling that nothing is worth the effort.

Productivity techniques alone rarely fix burnout when the causes are structural, such as unmanageable workload, lack of control or unclear expectations. Burnout symptoms can also overlap with depression, anxiety and physical health conditions. If symptoms persist, talk to a doctor or a qualified mental health professional. This entry is general information, not medical advice.
example: Illustrative example: A manager working 60-hour weeks for months feels exhausted even after weekends, is irritable with their team, and is making mistakes they never used to make. Tracking one week shows 22 hours spent in meetings. Declining or delegating 8 hours of low-value meetings and setting a firm finish time are structural changes. Seeing a doctor or counsellor if symptoms don't improve is the other half of the response.
common_mistake: Treating burnout as a personal weakness to push through with more caffeine and productivity hacks, instead of tackling workload, boundaries and recovery, and seeking professional help when needed.
title: Burnout
